"Bienvenue chez Innova-Tech ! Nous sommes une équipe passionnée et motivée, prête à relever les défis de l'édition 2026 duNASA Space Apps ChallengeàLibreville.

Notre approche combine créativité, rigueur technique et esprit d'innovation pour concevoir des solutions percutantes. Nous unissons nos compétences en code, analyse de données et design pour donner vie à un projet d'impact !"
summary:
EVA Planner is a mission copilot for astronauts walking on Mars. It plans, supervises and reviews an extravehicular activity (EVA) from a habitat to a geologic target in Jezero crater, using real orbital data: HiRISE imagery and 1 m elevation, CRISM mineralogy and the USGS geologic map.

Before leaving, the team picks the target on the map or from candidate carbonate sites within walking range. An A* search finds the least-cost path, which avoids steep slopes and sand. The tool computes a single, transparent safety margin: autonomy minus outbound, observation and return time. Any plan that would break the safety reserve is refused.

During the walk, three synchronized views share one state: a habitat console, an astronaut tablet and a 3D helmet display built only from real terrain data. When an obstacle appears, the route is recomputed live, and options that would put the crew at risk are refused.

Mars exploration needs decisions that are fast, explainable and safe. EVA Planner turns scattered science datasets into one clear question: can we get there, do the science and come back with margin?
details:
What it does. EVA Planner supports a crewed walk on Mars from start to finish, from a habitat (A) to a science target (B) in Jezero crater.

  • Prepare: choose B by clicking the map or from a ranked list of candidate sites. Candidates are regions mapped as marginal carbonates by CRISM and reachable within the return budget, ranked by return time with area and margin. The app computes the route, elevation profile, slopes and durations, and shows where the astronaut can safely go.
  • Supervise: the habitat follows the simulated position, remaining autonomy and margin; sends messages to the helmet; and can replay the walk with a time cursor.
  • React: an obstacle can be placed on the map by the habitat or reported by the astronaut's tablet. The route is recomputed around it, with two options (go around and continue, or return home), each with its margin. Unsafe options are refused, and the decision is logged and shown in all three views.
  • Review: a full replay of the walk, geolocated observations and an exportable log.

How it works. We processed the data team's rasters into a 5 m terrain grid: elevation, slope, and a walking cost of (1 + 0.1 × slope°), doubled in sand, with slopes over 20° forbidden. The browser runs A* and Dijkstra on this grid. We checked them against the Python reference (scikit-image) to within 1%. Durations are terrain cost ÷ walking speed, and one margin formula is used everywhere. The return zone is computed live from the cost field. The helmet view is a three.js scene built from the HiRISE 1 m and 5 m DTMs, a CTX 20 m horizon and the HiRISE orthoimage, with the camera 1.7 m above the simulated position. Map tiles and terrain are cached locally, so the app works offline, and devices on the same local network stay synchronized.

Benefits and impact. One explainable safety number instead of scattered estimates; science targets ranked by what is reachable; incidents handled with recomputed, verified options; and the same picture for the crew and mission support. The approach can be reused for any site with a DTM and a science map.

Creativity. The tool links orbital science (where are the carbonates?) with operational safety (can we get there and back?) in a single interface, and turns real terrain data into a first-person helmet view without inventing any detail.

What we considered. Every value shows its provenance (observed, derived, simulated or interpretation). Durations and autonomy are clearly marked as demonstration parameters, not NASA standards. A carbonate signal is presented as a habitability clue, never as evidence of life. The views are designed for readability with gloves and helmets: large targets, a minimal HUD and colour-blind-aware cues.

Tools. TypeScript, React, Vite, Zustand, OpenLayers, three.js (@react-three/fiber, drei), Vitest and Playwright; Python (rasterio, pyproj, shapely, scikit-image, NumPy, Pillow).
